metadata.excerpt_139_words: Power, Inequality, and the Critique of International Law examines how international law both constrains power and reflects unequal histories, institutions, markets, and political voice. This article explains formal sovereign equality, empire, decolonization, sources doctrine, customary law, consent, Security Council hierarchy, selective enforcement, international economic law, debt, development, human rights, race, gender, migration, climate inequality, corporate power, expertise, adjudication, and institutional legitimacy. It shows how legal rules that appear neutral may operate differently across unequal states, communities, and economic positions. The article also addresses TWAIL, feminist international law, critical race approaches, political economy, and Global South critiques. By connecting doctrine, institutions, case studies, and lawyer-facing workflows, it shows how critique does not abandon international law, but asks whether global legality can become more equal, accountable, and emancipatory in practice today worldwide.
